claims.claim: Bela Barenyi patented the crumple-zone concept in 1952 and Mercedes-Benz introduced the first production car with crumple zones in 1959 (the W111)
claims.definition: Barényi's patent 854157 (filed 1952) describes a vehicle with a rigid passenger cell and deformable front and rear sections; the 1959 Mercedes-Benz W111 'tailfin' was the first production implementation
claims.authoritative_source: Mercedes-Benz Group corporate archive (Barényi biography, patent 854157); German Patent Office records

claims.claim: for the same change of momentum, spreading the stop over a longer time lowers the average force on the occupants (impulse-momentum: F_avg = Δp/Δt)
claims.definition: the impulse-momentum theorem: average net force equals momentum change divided by stop time; doubling the pulse duration halves the average deceleration force
claims.authoritative_source: standard mechanics (Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, impulse-momentum chapter)

claims.claim: crumple zones convert crash kinetic energy into plastic deformation of deliberately engineered fold structures, so the metal — not the occupants — absorbs the energy
claims.definition: designed longitudinal members fold in a controlled sequence; plastic hinges dissipate energy that would otherwise go into occupant acceleration or cabin intrusion
claims.authoritative_source: vehicle crashworthiness literature (e.g. Huang, 'Vehicle Crash Mechanics'); IIHS crash-protection explainers

claims.claim: modern cars pair deformable crush zones with a high-strength passenger cell designed to keep the survival space intact during the crush
claims.definition: the safety cage uses high-strength/ultra-high-strength steel in the pillars and floor members while the front and rear structures are engineered to collapse
claims.authoritative_source: IIHS crashworthinessTopic explanations; vehicle body-structure engineering references

claims.claim: a crush structure that extends the crash pulse lowers occupant deceleration: roughly doubling the stopping time halves the average deceleration for the same velocity change
claims.definition: consequence of the impulse-momentum theorem applied to the crash pulse; crumple distance buys stop time
claims.measured_value: directional physics; exact factor depends on the pulse shape
claims.authoritative_source: standard mechanics plus crash-pulse literature (Huang, 'Vehicle Crash Mechanics')

claims.claim: pre-crumple-era designs aimed to resist deformation, and that rigidity transmitted sharp deceleration spikes and cabin intrusion to occupants
claims.definition: stiff structures stop the cabin quickly (short pulse, high force) and leave little crush space; mid-century crash data motivated the deformable-cell philosophy
claims.authoritative_source: IIHS crashworthiness history; crash-safety engineering literature

claims.claim: restraints are staged inside the crash pulse: belt pretensioners tighten first and airbags inflate within tens of milliseconds, supplementing the crush structure
claims.definition: airbag inflation typically completes on the order of 30-50 ms after trigger, within the roughly 100 ms frontal pulse; exact timings vary by vehicle and crash severity
claims.measured_value: airbag inflation commonly cited ~30-50 ms; frontal pulse ~100 ms (varies)
claims.authoritative_source: NHTSA airbag documentation; SAE crash-pulse literature (timings vary — hedged)
